name: Cista++
workload: Serialize/deserialize/traverse a graph of nodes and edges (object-oriented graph with pointers/indices) using the 'offset' and 'raw' variants of Cista++, compared to cereal, Cap'n Proto, and FlatBuffers
claimed_speedup: Cista++ 'offset': serialize 4ms vs cereal 216ms (~54x), deserialize 0.16ms vs cereal 111ms (~694x), deserialize+traverse 66ms vs cereal 174ms (~2.6x); compile time (clang-7) 1.351s vs cereal 1.827s
tradeoffs: The zero-copy 'offset' variant requires reading/writing in a fixed pointer-offset layout (no relocation), so both ends must share pointer width/endianness; the 'raw' variant (native pointers, relocatable) is far slower to serialize (3555ms) because of the extra relocation pass. Not schema-evolution-friendly like protobuf/capnproto without opt-in versioning.
caveats: Benchmark numbers come from felixguendling's own companion repo (cpp-serialization-benchmark), so it is first-party, but methodology (code, compiler, OS, exact CPU) is fully public, which is why it still qualifies for tier A. The main cista README shows a second run of the same benchmark with different absolute numbers (72ms vs 239ms serialize) from a different session; both point the same direction. The very large deserialize speedup vs cereal is an architectural effect of zero-copy access (no parsing step), not a benchmarking artifact.

name: bitsery
workload: Serialize/deserialize a nested 'Monster' struct (vectors, strings, enums, weapons) for 300,000 samples, compiled with GCC 11 and Clang 12.0.1 on Ubuntu 20.04 x64 (fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark suite)
claimed_speedup: bitsery 1119-1524ms ser / 1166-1561ms des vs boost 15126-16011ms ser / 12724-13017ms des (~10-14x faster), and vs cereal 9977-10777ms ser / 8565-9088ms des (~7-9x faster)
hardware: Ubuntu 20.04 x64 (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: No implicit metadata/schema (compile-time only serialize() functions must be written per type); forward/backward compatibility and polymorphism require opting into specific extensions rather than being automatic like Boost.Serialization's archive system.
caveats: The benchmark repo is maintained by bitsery's own author (fraillt), so it is a first-party comparison; the report states compiler and OS but not the exact CPU model, which per the tiering rules caps this at tier C rather than A/B despite the large, plausible-looking margin.

name: struct_pack (yalantinglibs)
workload: Serialize/deserialize three struct shapes (a 4-field 'rect', a 4-field 'person', and a nested 'Monster'-style struct) for one million iterations each, compared to protobuf, msgpack, and flatbuffers, using compile-time reflection (no macros for aggregate types)
claimed_speedup: (derived from page data, read off the serialize-speed chart) struct_pack ~15-20ns vs protobuf ~320ns for 'rect' (~16-20x), ~120ns vs ~530ns for 'person' (~4.4x), ~650ns vs ~2900ns for 'monster' (~4.5x); also far ahead of msgpack (~1100-8000ns) on the same cases
tradeoffs: Works best on aggregate structs; non-aggregate types (private members, custom order) need the YLT_REFL macro. Forward/backward compatibility requires explicitly wrapping new fields in struct_pack::compatible<T,version>. Ships as part of a large multi-library monorepo (yalantinglibs) rather than a standalone single-purpose dependency.
caveats: Numbers were read visually off bar charts (PNG images) in the docs rather than a text table, so the figures above are estimates from the chart axes, not exact values; confidence is lowered accordingly. The docs compare against protobuf/msgpack/flatbuffers, not Boost.Serialization or cereal directly, hence baseline_in_list=false.

name: YAS (Yet Another Serialization)
workload: thekvs/cpp-serializers: serialize/deserialize a mixed object 1,000,000 times, averaged over 50 runs; fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark: serialize/deserialize a nested 'Monster' struct 300,000 times
claimed_speedup: thekvs suite: yas 302.7ms total vs boost 1195.04ms (~3.9x) and cereal 1052.46ms (~3.5x); fraillt suite (GCC 11): yas 2286ms ser/1770ms des vs boost 15126ms/12724ms (~6.6x/~7.2x) and cereal 10777ms/9088ms (~4.7x/~5.1x)
compiler_and_flags: thekvs suite: C++14, tested with Clang/GCC, Release build (exact compiler used for the published table not pinned down); fraillt suite: GCC 11 / Clang 12.0.1, Release
hardware: thekvs: unspecified 'Intel Core i7' desktop, Ubuntu 16.04; fraillt: Ubuntu 20.04 x64, exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: No LICENSE file in the repository, so there is no explicit permission to reuse/modify the code despite it being publicly readable; project has had low commit activity in the last ~1.5 years.
caveats: yas's own README states it was created specifically 'as a replacement of boost.serialization because of its insufficient speed' and cites both benchmark repos used here. Both cited benchmarks are run by third parties (not yas's author), which supports tier B, but neither pins an exact CPU model, so tier is capped below A. No license file was found in the repo or README, so usability is recorded as 'reference' rather than 'copyable'.

name: YaFF (Yet another Flat Format)
workload: Median time to read every field of a serialized message: flat messages of 10/100 uint64 fields, and a 3-level hierarchical message under hot (cache-resident, ~2KB) and cold (random, ~512MB working set) access patterns, using google/benchmark
claimed_speedup: YaFF's Flat Layout is ahead of Protobuf by x25-50 on flat messages, x25 faster than Protobuf under hierarchical hot access (within 1.2x of a raw C++ struct), and about 2x faster than Protobuf even under cold/random access; also x2-3.5x faster than FlatBuffers across these cases
stars_or_usage: 531 stars; new project published by Yandex
tradeoffs: Requires an existing .proto schema (it is an alternate physical layout for Protobuf messages, not a fully independent wire format); dynamic/adaptive layout selection between Flat and Sparse adds complexity versus a single fixed layout; very new project so format/API stability is far less proven than Protobuf or FlatBuffers.
caveats: Very new, fast-moving repository (first public benchmarks appear recent). The docs note absolute numbers depend on CPU/memory but claim relative ratios should hold across hardware. GitHub's automatic license detection reports NOASSERTION even though the README badge and LICENSE file state Apache-2.0.

name: Fast Binary Encoding (FBE)
workload: Serialize/deserialize a fixed Account/Wallet/Order domain model using the CppBenchmark harness; message size ~120-280 bytes depending on format
claimed_speedup: FBE serialize 66ns / deserialize 82ns vs Protobuf serialize 628ns / deserialize 759ns (~9.5x / ~9.3x faster); also faster than Cap'n Proto (558/359ns) and FlatBuffers (830/290ns) in the same comparison table
compiler_and_flags: Not stated exactly; CppBenchmark report lists 'Process configuration: release' but no compiler name/version/flags
tradeoffs: Requires its own IDL/schema and a code generator (similar to protobuf/Cap'n Proto), rather than serializing plain C++ structs directly; the linked benchmark uses a small, fixed message (~100-280 bytes), which may not reflect large-payload behavior.
caveats: FastBinaryEncoding and the comparison repo (CppSerialization) share the same author (chronoxor), so this is a first-party benchmark; the CppBenchmark report states CPU model and OS but omits the exact compiler and flags, which caps this at tier C rather than A.
